title: Cellulitis & erysipelas
summary: Spreading dermal infection, usually in one leg. Exclude the mimics, draw the border, give flucloxacillin for 5–7 days and safety-net hard. Bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis.

glance.think: Acute, unilateral, hot, red, swollen, tender skin, often on the lower leg, with or without fever. Erysipelas has a sharp, raised edge.
glance.engine: Streptococci (± S. aureus) entering through a skin break such as a fissured toe web, ulcer or eczema.
glance.backbone: Mark the border, elevate, give analgesia, flucloxacillin 5–7 days, and treat the portal of entry.
glance.never_miss: Necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion), sepsis and orbital cellulitis.

what: In practice the two overlap and are managed the same way in primary care.

list: A **breach in the skin barrier** lets bacteria in. Common entry points are **tinea pedis**, eczema, ulcers, trauma, bites, lymphoedema and previous surgery.
Bacteria spread through the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, with or without lymphangitis.
The host inflammatory response causes the redness, heat, swelling and systemic symptoms.
Risk factors: obesity, venous insufficiency, lymphoedema, diabetes, and previous cellulitis.

head: Patient
Usual organisms (Module 5)
rows: A broader range, including **Gram-negatives**, so take advice

list: **Cellulitis:** expanding redness, heat, swelling and tenderness, usually in **one** leg. May have fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy and lymphangitic streaking. Can have blisters.
**Erysipelas:** bright red, hot, **raised, sharply demarcated** plaque, often on the face or leg. Fever and chills are common and may come before the rash.
**Skin of colour:** redness is much less obvious, so rely on **swelling, warmth, pain and induration**.
Look for **peau d’orange**, bullae, purpura, **lymphangitic streaks** and tender regional lymph nodes.
Fever and rigors can come **before** the rash.

features.title: Milian’s ear sign
features.text: Redness involving the **pinna** favours **erysipelas** over cellulitis. The ear has no deep dermis or subcutaneous fat, so deep cellulitis cannot really involve it.

list: **Clinical.** Exclude non-infective mimics before giving antibiotics.
**Mark the border** with a skin pen and record the date and time. Photograph if possible, to monitor spread.
Assess severity: observations, NEWS2 or sepsis screen, comorbidities and site (face or periorbital).
Swab only if there is broken skin with a penetrating injury, water exposure, or infection acquired outside the UK.
Bloods and blood cultures belong in the hospital pathway for unwell patients.

head: Mimic
Distinguishing clues
rows: Often **bilateral**, chronic, itchy or scaly, little pain, no fever
Calf swelling and tenderness, less skin redness; Wells score, D-dimer or Doppler
Joint-centred; very tender; history of attacks
Itch more than pain; central punctum; rapid onset
Itchy, vesicular or scaly; matches exposure; no fever
Fish or meat handlers; finger or hand; violaceous
Painful, woody, red gaiter skin, often bilateral or recurrent; frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis
Long history of swelling; less acute

differentials.title: Necrotising fasciitis
differentials.text: Severe **pain out of proportion** to the signs, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, dusky or purple skin, bullae or crepitus. This is an **emergency**: 999 or ED.

list: Draw around the edge, elevate the limb, give analgesia and encourage fluids.
Use emollient for dry skin. **Avoid compression** during acute cellulitis.
**Treat the portal of entry:** tinea pedis, eczema, ulcers, lymphoedema.

head: Situation
Choice
rows: **Flucloxacillin** 500 mg–1 g four times daily for **5–7 days** (longer if clinically needed)
Clarithromycin, doxycycline or erythromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy)
Near the eyes or nose (periorbital / ‘danger triangle’)
**Co-amoxiclav** (penicillin allergy: clarithromycin + metronidazole). Consider specialist advice
Severe, or unable to take oral
IV in hospital or the community IV service; review switch to oral by 48 hours

list: **Reassess** if worse at any time, or not improving after **2–3 days**.
Recurrent cellulitis (2 or more episodes in 12 months): a specialist may consider prophylaxis (e.g. phenoxymethylpenicillin). This is not routine in primary care.

management.title: Recurrent cellulitis
management.text: Two or more episodes: treat the portals of entry (tinea pedis, eczema), manage oedema with compression once the acute episode has settled, and discuss prophylactic penicillin with a clinician (based on the PATCH trials).

red_flags: **Necrotising fasciitis signs:** pain out of proportion, rapid spread, purple bullae, crepitus, or a very unwell patient. **Emergency.**
**Sepsis:** low blood pressure, raised heart or breathing rate, confusion, mottled skin.
**Periorbital or orbital cellulitis:** pain on eye movement, proptosis, reduced vision. Same-day ophthalmology or ED.
Rapid spread beyond the marked border, or failure after 48–72 hours of oral therapy.
Infants, frail older adults, the immunocompromised, or significant lymphoedema: lower threshold to refer.
pearls: **Bilateral red legs are not cellulitis until proven otherwise.** Think venous eczema or lipodermatosclerosis.
The skin takes **days** to look normal after the bacteria are controlled. Residual redness on day 3 is not automatic failure, so avoid reflexively extending the course.
**Always treat athlete’s foot** to reduce recurrent leg cellulitis.
On the face, have a lower threshold for review or admission.
Safety-net: rapid worsening, severe pain, purple blisters or feeling faint means same-day emergency care.
At 48–72 hours, if it is not better: swab any open wound, consider MRSA, and **revisit the diagnosis**.
